extracted.intended_audience: literary reviewers, critics, and creative writers (poets and prose writers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for conducting literary reviews and for compositional practice in poetry and prose: how a review should be founded and executed, what to include and avoid, and craft advice for poets (use of nature, memory vs imagination, metre, and stylistic formation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Review based on a published code of principles
rubrics_metrics.description: A review should be started upon a published code of principles, critical, moral, political, and religious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewer should launch a periodical founded on an explicit code of principles that states its critical/moral/political/religious stance up front, so readers know the governing standards of judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Announce scope of what will be reviewed
rubrics_metrics.description: The review should announce what sort of books it would review, namely works of literature as contradistinguished from all that offspring of the press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make clear before the review begins which classes of works will be treated (e.g., 'works of literature' rather than ephemeral press products or mere advertisings for circulating libraries). This clarifies purpose and avoids conflating literature with mass press output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give a fair account of the author's intention
rubrics_metrics.description: The review should really give a fair account of what the author intended to do, and in his own words, if possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarize the author's aims accurately; where feasible, quote the author or paraphrase in a way that represents the author's intention faithfully rather than imposing the reviewer's agenda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include specimens of execution
rubrics_metrics.description: A review should afford one or two fair specimens of the execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide short extracts or examples from the work under review so readers can judge style and manner of execution for themselves rather than relying solely on the reviewer's description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never descend to personality
rubrics_metrics.description: The review itself must never descend for one moment to any personality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ad hominem attacks and personal invective; criticism should target the work, its methods and execution, not the author's character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide foundational, powerful articles before launch
rubrics_metrics.description: Before commencement, the review should be provided with a dozen powerful articles upon fundamental topics to appear in succession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish authority and set the intellectual tone by preparing a sequence of substantial foundational essays addressing core topics; this helps define the review's voice and standards from the start.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer a mean between essayizing and old-style reviewing
rubrics_metrics.description: A mean between the two extremes (old-style reviewing and essay writing) still remains to be taken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the extremes of mere advertisement/press notices and entirely personal essayizing; balance fair, principled critical appraisal with broader essayistic context where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study sacred texts to avoid vulgarity of style
rubrics_metrics.description: Intense study of the Bible will keep any writer from being vulgar, in point of style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular, close study of revered, rhetorically rich texts (the Bible in this example) cultivates diction, avoids vulgarity, and elevates stylistic taste in writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic borrowing should repay what is taken
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet ought not to pick nature's pocket: let him borrow, and so borrow as to repay by the very act of borrowing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a poet uses elements from nature, myth, or prior works, the poet must transform or enrich them so that the act of borrowing returns value (i.e., produce original insight, transformation, or restitution rather than mere appropriation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine nature accurately; write from recollection; trust imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine nature accurately, but write from recollection; and trust more to your imagination than to your memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe nature carefully to gather material, but compose from remembered impressions filtered through imagination. This preserves freshness and unity in representation rather than slavish transcription.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metre should be musical, not merely gymnastic exercise
rubrics_metrics.description: Really the metre of some of the modern poems I have read, bears about the same relation to metre properly understood, that dumb bells do to music; both are for exercise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meter must serve musical and expressive ends; avoid rhythmic patterns that are merely mechanical or technical exercises lacking musicality and expressive appropriateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish purposes: rhetoric persuades, logic convicts, grammar signifies
rubrics_metrics.description: The object of rhetoric is persuasion,--of logic, conviction,--of grammar, significancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing or judging writing, identify the principal aim (to persuade, to convince logically, or to ensure clarity of signification) and apply the appropriate standards and techniques; be mindful that sentences also have a distinct rhetorical/‘rhematic’ function (the 'logic of sentences').

rubrics_metrics.name: Value criterional (premiss-based) logic over over-elaborate syllogistics
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two kinds of logic: 1. Syllogistic. 2. Criterional. The criterional logic, or logic of premisses, is, of course, much the most important; and it has never yet been treated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overreliance on artificial forms of syllogistic exercises; give priority to assessing and constructing sound premises (criteria) that ground arguments—the logic of premises is the substantive part of reasoning.
